prompt: Order the causal chain when the Federal Reserve buys government bonds.

options.text: Market interest rates fall across the economy
Federal Reserve buys Treasury bonds on the open market
Business investment and aggregate demand rise
Commercial bank reserves and money supply expand

explanation: Fed bond purchases add reserves to banks, which lowers interest rates and boosts investment and output.

trap_notes.default: Open-market purchases expand bank reserves first, pushing rates down and then lifting investment.

prompt: Order the causal chain of contractionary open-market bond sales.

options.text: Commercial bank reserves shrink
Borrowing and inflation pressures cool down
Central bank sells government bonds to banks
Short-term and lending interest rates rise

explanation: Selling bonds drains reserves from banks, raising interest rates and slowing borrowing and inflation.

trap_notes.default: Bond sales pull cash out of banks, which raises rates before slowing spending and inflation.

prompt: Order the causal chain after Congress cuts personal income tax rates.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts right and real GDP rises
Households have higher disposable income
Congress enacts broad personal income tax cuts
Consumer spending on goods and services grows

explanation: Lower income taxes leave households with more take-home pay, increasing consumption and shifting aggregate demand right.

trap_notes.default: Tax cuts raise disposable income first, which fuels consumer spending and then aggregate demand.

prompt: Order the causal steps of the crowding-out effect from deficit spending.

options.text: Real interest rates climb in credit markets
Private business investment spending declines
Government borrows heavily to cover a budget deficit
Total demand for loanable funds increases

explanation: Heavy government borrowing raises demand for loanable funds, driving up real interest rates and crowding out private investment.

trap_notes.default: Deficit borrowing raises loanable-funds demand and interest rates before reducing private investment.

prompt: Order the causal chain of cost-push inflation from an energy shock.

options.text: Short-run aggregate supply shifts to the left
Global crude oil prices spike sharply
Economy experiences higher prices and lower output
Shipping and manufacturing costs rise for firms

explanation: Higher oil prices raise production costs, shifting short-run aggregate supply left and causing stagflation.

trap_notes.default: Input-cost spikes shift aggregate supply left, raising the price level while reducing output.

prompt: Order the causal chain of demand-pull inflation in a booming economy.

options.text: Total spending outpaces factory production capacity
Overall consumer price level climbs across markets
Economy approaches full employment and output
Firms raise prices to ration scarce goods

explanation: At full employment, excess spending strains capacity, prompting firms to raise prices and lifting the overall price level.

trap_notes.default: Demand-pull inflation starts with spending exceeding full-employment capacity, driving prices up.

prompt: Order the causal chain of a binding rent ceiling on city apartments.

options.text: Chronic housing shortage develops in the city
City sets maximum rent below market equilibrium
Waitlists and non-price rationing emerge
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied

explanation: A rent cap below equilibrium makes quantity demanded exceed supply, creating a shortage and non-price rationing.

trap_notes.default: Below-equilibrium caps create excess demand, which causes a persistent shortage and waitlists.

prompt: Order the causal chain of a binding agricultural price floor.

options.text: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Government buys and stores excess farm crops
Government sets minimum crop price above equilibrium
Persistent grain surplus builds in markets

explanation: A price floor above equilibrium encourages excess supply, creating a surplus that the state often buys.

trap_notes.default: Above-equilibrium floors make quantity supplied exceed demand, generating a market surplus.

prompt: Order the causal chain when an excise tax hits an inelastic good.

options.text: Retail price rises by nearly the full tax amount
Government levies a per-pack tax on cigarettes
Buyers bear most of the economic tax burden
Supply curve shifts upward by the tax size

explanation: Taxing an inelastic good shifts supply up, pushing retail prices sharply higher so buyers bear most of the tax.

trap_notes.default: When demand is inelastic, sellers pass most of a supply-shifting tax onto consumers through higher prices.

prompt: Order the causal chain after a nation imposes a tariff on imported steel.

options.text: Imported steel prices jump for domestic buyers
Domestic steel mills expand output and sales
Government places a 25 percent tariff on steel imports
Consumers face higher prices for metal products

explanation: A tariff raises the price of imported steel, letting domestic mills sell more while raising downstream consumer prices.

trap_notes.default: Tariffs raise import prices first, shielding domestic producers but raising costs for buyers.

prompt: Order the causal chain when a nation's currency depreciates.

options.text: Foreign buyers purchase more of the nation's goods
Domestic currency falls in value on forex markets
Nation's net exports and aggregate demand increase
Domestic exports become cheaper for foreign buyers

explanation: A weaker currency makes exports cheaper abroad, boosting foreign orders and increasing net exports.

trap_notes.default: Currency depreciation lowers export prices in foreign terms, lifting export volume and net exports.

prompt: Order the causal chain from a domestic interest-rate hike to exchange rates.

options.text: Foreign investors seek higher bond yields locally
Demand for the domestic currency rises in forex markets
Domestic currency appreciates against foreign rivals
Central bank raises domestic benchmark interest rates

explanation: Higher domestic rates attract foreign capital inflows, raising demand for the currency and causing it to appreciate.

trap_notes.default: Higher interest rates draw foreign capital, increasing currency demand and appreciating the exchange rate.

prompt: Order how fractional-reserve banking expands the money supply.

options.text: Bank lends excess reserves to new borrowers
Customer deposits cash into a checking account
Total money supply grows by a deposit multiplier
Bank sets aside a fraction as required reserves

explanation: A deposit lets a bank hold required reserves and lend the rest, creating new deposits that multiply the money supply.

trap_notes.default: Banks receive deposits, hold required reserves, lend excess reserves, and repeat the cycle.

prompt: Order the causal chain of a classic commercial bank run.

options.text: Bank exhausts its liquid cash reserves
Depositors fear the bank may become insolvent
Bank fails without central bank emergency loans
Customers rush to withdraw all their deposits at once

explanation: Fear of insolvency sparks simultaneous withdrawals, draining liquid reserves and forcing bank failure without a lender.

trap_notes.default: Loss of confidence triggers mass withdrawals, which drain cash reserves and cause insolvency.

prompt: Order the causal chain that produces a hyperinflation spiral.

options.text: People spend cash immediately before it loses value
Rapidly rising money velocity drives prices skyward
Government prints vast money to pay budget deficits
Currency loses purchasing power rapidly

explanation: Printing money for deficits erodes its value, causing people to spend cash faster and accelerating price increases.

trap_notes.default: Monetizing deficits erodes currency value first, which speeds up spending and sends prices soaring.

prompt: Order the causal chain of a wage-price inflation spiral.

options.text: Workers demand higher nominal wages to catch up
Firms raise product prices to cover higher payrolls
Rising living costs erode workers' real wages
Economy experiences accelerating price inflation

explanation: Eroded real wages prompt workers to seek raises, pushing firms to hike prices and fueling further inflation.

trap_notes.default: Falling real wages spark wage demands, which raise business costs and lead to higher prices.

prompt: Order how human capital investment drives long-run economic growth.

options.text: Workforce acquires stronger technical and job skills
Nation expands funding for schools and job training
Long-run real GDP per capita rises steadily
Output per worker hour increases across industries

explanation: Education funding builds worker skills, raising labor productivity and lifting long-run real GDP per capita.

trap_notes.default: Schooling builds skills, skills raise productivity per worker, and productivity drives per-capita GDP.

prompt: Order the causal chain of Joseph Schumpeter's creative destruction.

options.text: Legacy firms using older methods lose market share
Entrepreneurs introduce a lower-cost technology
Labor and capital shift into newer growing sectors
Outdated businesses downsize or exit the market

explanation: New innovations undercut legacy firms, forcing outdated businesses to exit and freeing resources for newer sectors.

trap_notes.default: Innovation comes first, outcompeting legacy firms and reallocating resources to new industries.

prompt: Order how a Pigouvian tax corrects a negative pollution externality.

options.text: Social cost of production exceeds private firm cost
Government imposes a tax per ton of emissions
Factory pollutes a nearby river during production
Firm reduces output toward the socially efficient level

explanation: Unpriced pollution makes social cost exceed private cost; a per-unit emissions tax aligns output with social efficiency.

trap_notes.default: The externality creates a gap between private and social cost, which the tax closes to reduce output.

prompt: Order the causal chain of the tragedy of the commons in a fishery.

options.text: Breeding fish population depletes faster than recovery
Each boat races to catch as many fish as possible
Total future harvest collapses for the whole fleet
Ocean fishery has open access without catch limits

explanation: Open access gives each boat an incentive to overfish, depleting the stock and collapsing future harvests.

trap_notes.default: Open access drives individual overharvesting, which depletes the shared resource and ruins future yields.

prompt: Order why the free-rider problem leads private markets to underprovide streetlights.

options.text: Private firms cannot earn profit from streetlights
Non-paying passersby cannot be excluded from light
Private market underprovides neighborhood streetlights
Streetlights are non-excludable public goods

explanation: Because streetlights are non-excludable, free riders enjoy them without paying, leaving firms unprofitable and underproviding them.

trap_notes.default: Non-excludability lets non-payers benefit, removing private profit and causing underprovision.

prompt: Order the causal chain of adverse selection in the used-car market.

options.text: Owners of reliable cars withdraw from the market
Buyers cannot tell good used cars from defective ones
Mostly defective lemons remain available for sale
Buyers offer only an average price for all used cars

explanation: Hidden quality forces buyers to offer average prices, driving out good sellers and leaving mostly lemons.

trap_notes.default: Asymmetric information lowers buyer offers, which pushes good cars out and leaves defective ones.

prompt: Order the causal chain of moral hazard in auto insurance.

options.text: Driver takes fewer precautions against theft or dents
Financial risk of vehicle loss shifts to the insurer
Driver purchases a zero-deductible full-coverage policy
Insurer faces higher accident and claim payouts

explanation: Full coverage shifts loss risk to the insurer, reducing driver caution and raising total insurance claims.

trap_notes.default: Moral hazard happens after a contract is signed: shifted risk reduces caution and raises claims.

prompt: Order how comparative advantage generates mutual gains from trade.

options.text: Combined world production of both goods expands
Countries trade surplus goods at mutually beneficial terms
Each nation specializes in its lowest opportunity-cost good
Both nations consume beyond their domestic frontiers

explanation: Specializing by lowest opportunity cost expands total output, allowing trade to lift both nations beyond domestic limits.

trap_notes.default: Specialization comes first, expanding total output so trade lets both partners consume more.

prompt: Order the causal chain when the price of a substitute good doubles.

options.text: Tea looks relatively cheaper than morning coffee
Demand curve for tea shifts to the right
Poor harvest causes retail coffee prices to double
Consumers switch from buying coffee to buying tea

explanation: Higher coffee prices make tea relatively cheaper, prompting consumers to switch and shifting tea demand right.

trap_notes.default: A higher price for a substitute makes the alternative look cheaper, shifting its demand curve right.

prompt: Order the causal chain when the price of a complementary good falls.

options.text: Demand curve for replacement ink cartridges shifts right
More households purchase home inkjet printers
Equilibrium price and sales of ink cartridges rise
Retail price of home printers drops sharply

explanation: Cheaper printers boost printer purchases, which shifts demand for complementary ink cartridges right and raises ink sales.

trap_notes.default: When a complement gets cheaper, people buy more of it and increase demand for its paired good.

prompt: Order the long-run adjustment in a perfectly competitive market.

options.text: New rival firms enter the profitable industry
Market price falls until economic profit reaches zero
Existing firms earn positive economic profits
Industry supply curve shifts to the right

explanation: Positive profits attract new entrants, shifting market supply right and driving price down to zero economic profit.

trap_notes.default: Economic profits attract entry, which increases supply and drives long-run price back to break-even.

prompt: Order how an unregulated monopoly creates deadweight loss.

options.text: Monopoly price rises above marginal production cost
Single firm restricts output to maximize profit
Total economic surplus shrinks below competitive level
Mutually beneficial trades between buyers and firm vanish

explanation: Restricting output lifts price above marginal cost, eliminating mutually beneficial trades and shrinking total surplus.

trap_notes.default: Monopolies restrict output first, pushing price above marginal cost and causing lost trades.

prompt: Order the causal chain of diminishing marginal returns in a factory.

options.text: Each additional worker adds less extra output
Factory hires more workers with fixed machinery
Marginal cost of producing each extra unit rises
Workers crowd around limited machines and space

explanation: Adding labor to fixed machines causes crowding, reducing each new worker's extra output and raising marginal cost.

trap_notes.default: Fixed capital gets crowded as labor rises, lowering marginal product and pushing marginal cost up.

prompt: Order the standard competitive-market chain of a binding minimum wage.

options.text: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds labor demanded
Employers hire fewer entry-level workers
Government sets minimum wage above market equilibrium
Surplus of unemployed job seekers develops

explanation: A wage floor above equilibrium creates excess labor supply as firms hire fewer workers, producing a labor surplus.

trap_notes.default: In a competitive model, a wage floor above equilibrium reduces hiring and leaves excess labor supply.

prompt: Order the causal chain of derived demand in the labor market.

options.text: Automakers expand battery factory production
Wages for battery engineers rise in the labor market
Consumers buy far more electric vehicles
Firms increase demand to hire battery engineers

explanation: Higher consumer demand for EVs pushes automakers to expand production, raising demand and wages for battery engineers.

trap_notes.default: Labor demand is derived from product demand: consumers buy goods first, then firms hire workers.

prompt: Order how automatic stabilizers cushion an economic downturn.

options.text: Household incomes fall and layoffs increase
Decline in aggregate consumer spending is softened
Tax bills drop while unemployment benefits rise
Economy enters a sharp cyclical recession

explanation: During a recession, falling incomes automatically lower tax payments and trigger unemployment aid, cushioning spending.

trap_notes.default: Recession lowers incomes first, automatically cutting taxes and raising benefits without new laws.

prompt: Order the causal chain of Irving Fisher's deflationary debt spiral.

options.text: Real burden of fixed dollar debts rises sharply
Aggregate demand and output fall even further
Overall consumer and producer prices fall steadily
Debtors slash spending to repay heavier loans

explanation: Falling prices raise the real burden of fixed debts, forcing borrowers to cut spending and deepening the downturn.

trap_notes.default: Deflation makes fixed debts heavier in real terms, forcing spending cuts that shrink demand further.

prompt: Order the causal chain of a Keynesian liquidity trap.

options.text: Households and banks hoard cash instead of lending
Short-term nominal interest rates hit near zero
Fiscal spending becomes needed to lift demand
Extra money injections fail to lower rates further

explanation: Near zero rates, people hoard cash so extra money fails to stimulate lending, leaving fiscal policy as the main tool.

trap_notes.default: At the zero lower bound, cash hoarding blunts conventional rate cuts, elevating fiscal policy.

prompt: Order how Quantitative Easing works when policy rates hit zero.

options.text: Long-term bond prices rise and yields fall
Mortgage and corporate borrowing costs ease
Short-term policy rate reaches the zero lower bound
Central bank buys long-term Treasuries and MBS

explanation: With short-term rates at zero, central banks buy long-term assets to lower long-term yields and ease mortgage rates.

trap_notes.default: QE begins at the zero bound by purchasing long-term bonds, which lowers long-term yields and borrowing costs.

prompt: Order the causal chain of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff spiral.

options.text: Foreign trading partners pass retaliatory tariffs
U.S. Congress raises tariffs on twenty thousand goods
Global downturn and U.S. farm crisis deepen
World trade volumes collapse by roughly two-thirds

explanation: Smoot-Hawley provoked foreign retaliation, collapsing world trade volumes and worsening the Great Depression.

trap_notes.default: U.S. tariff hikes triggered foreign retaliation, which shrank global trade and deepened the slump.

prompt: Order how the 1930s gold standard worsened the Great Depression.

options.text: Domestic money supply and credit contract sharply
Central bank hikes interest rates to defend gold peg
Deflation and unemployment worsen across the economy
Country experiences gold outflows during a crisis

explanation: To stop gold outflows, central banks raised rates, contracting the money supply and worsening deflation.

trap_notes.default: Gold outflows forced central banks to hike rates during a slump, shrinking credit and deepening deflation.

prompt: Order the causal chain of the 1973 OPEC oil embargo.

options.text: Global crude oil supply drops sharply
OPEC members cut output and embargo Western allies
Industrial economies suffer stagflation
Fuel, heating, and freight costs surge worldwide

explanation: OPEC's embargo slashed oil supply, driving up energy and freight costs and triggering 1970s stagflation.

trap_notes.default: The embargo cut supply first, spiking fuel costs before producing stagflation in industrial nations.

prompt: Order the causal chain of the 2008 U.S. subprime mortgage crisis.

options.text: U.S. home prices stall and begin falling nationwide
Mortgage-backed securities plunge in value at banks
Lenders issue high-risk subprime home mortgages
High-risk borrowers default on monthly payments

explanation: Loose subprime lending collided with falling home prices, sparking defaults that crushed mortgage-backed securities.

trap_notes.default: Subprime loans were issued first; falling home prices triggered defaults, which hit bank securities.

prompt: Order how a global supply-chain bottleneck drives retail inflation.

options.text: Factories lack key chips and parts to finish goods
Store inventories shrink while demand stays strong
Port closures and container delays stall shipping
Retail prices climb rapidly across consumer goods

explanation: Port delays starve factories of parts, shrinking store inventories and driving up retail prices.

trap_notes.default: Shipping delays cut factory parts first, which shrinks finished inventory and pushes retail prices up.

prompt: Order how population aging creates fiscal pressure on public budgets.

options.text: Ratio of active workers to retirees shrinks
Public pension and elder healthcare outlays grow
Birth rates decline while life expectancy rises
Government budget deficits face upward pressure

explanation: Lower birth rates and longer lives shrink the worker-to-retiree ratio, raising pension costs and straining budgets.

trap_notes.default: Demographic shifts alter the worker-retiree ratio first, increasing pension and health spending.

prompt: Order how microfinance loans support rural entrepreneurship.

options.text: Tailor buys a sewing machine to expand output
Microfinance lender offers a small uncollateralized loan
Low-income villager lacks collateral for a bank loan
Household income and loan repayment capacity grow

explanation: Without traditional collateral, small microfinance loans let villagers buy tools and raise household income.

trap_notes.default: Microfinance addresses missing collateral by funding small tools that raise borrower earnings.

prompt: Order how secure property rights boost agricultural productivity.

options.text: Farmers trust they will keep future crop returns
Owners invest in irrigation and soil improvements
Government enforces clear legal land titles
Farm yields and rural incomes rise over time

explanation: Clear land titles assure farmers they will keep future gains, spurring long-term investment and higher yields.

trap_notes.default: Secure titles build confidence in future returns, which motivates capital investment and raises yields.

prompt: Order the causal chain of a fixed exchange-rate peg collapse.

options.text: Central bank sells foreign reserves to defend peg
Speculators bet against the currency as reserves fall
Currency peg becomes overvalued against the dollar
Government abandons peg and lets currency float

explanation: Defending an overvalued peg drains foreign reserves, inviting speculative attacks that force a float.

trap_notes.default: An overvalued peg drains reserves first; once reserves run low, speculation forces a float.

prompt: Order how a carbon cap-and-trade program cuts emissions.

options.text: Firms receive or buy tradable emission permits
Low-cost cleaners cut emissions and sell spare permits
Regulator sets an overall legal cap on total carbon
Total industry emissions fall at lowest social cost

explanation: A regulator caps total emissions and issues tradable permits, letting low-cost firms cut more and sell spare permits.

trap_notes.default: Cap-and-trade sets the total cap first, allocates permits, and uses trading to cut at lowest cost.

prompt: Sort each adult into the U.S. labor force or outside the labor force.
explanation: The labor force counts employed people and unemployed people actively seeking work; retirees and non-seeking students are outside it.

trap_notes.default: Active job seekers are counted in the labor force; retirees and students not looking for work are not.

prompt: Sort each profit feature under accounting profit or economic profit.
explanation: Accounting profit subtracts only explicit cash costs; economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs.

trap_notes.default: Economic profit includes opportunity costs, so it is smaller than accounting profit.

items.text: New sedan sold to a family
Sheet steel sold to an automaker
Loaf of bread bought at market
Flour bought by a commercial bakery

prompt: Sort each item as a final good or an intermediate good for GDP.
explanation: Final goods are sold to end users and counted in GDP; intermediate goods are used up making other goods.

trap_notes.default: GDP excludes intermediate inputs like bakery flour or automaker steel to avoid double counting.

prompt: Sort each financial instrument or trait into money or capital markets.
explanation: Money markets trade short-term debt maturing within a year; capital markets trade stocks and long-term bonds.

trap_notes.default: Money markets handle short-term liquidity under one year; capital markets handle long-term investment.

prompt: Sort each business combination as a horizontal or vertical merger.
explanation: Horizontal mergers combine direct competitors; vertical mergers combine firms at different supply-chain stages.

trap_notes.default: Horizontal means same stage (competitors); vertical means buyer and supplier along the production chain.

prompt: Sort each macroeconomic condition under stagflation or deflation.
explanation: Stagflation pairs high inflation with slow growth and joblessness; deflation is a sustained fall in the overall price level.

trap_notes.default: Stagflation means prices rise during a slump; deflation means overall prices fall.

items.text: Caused by a change in own price
Caused by a change in buyer tastes

prompt: Sort each change as a demand curve shift or a movement along the curve.
explanation: A change in the good's own price moves along the demand curve; income or tastes shift the entire curve.

trap_notes.default: Own-price changes move along a fixed curve; non-price determinants like income shift the curve.

items.text: Caused by product sale price rise
Caused by higher raw material cost

prompt: Sort each change as a supply curve shift or a movement along the curve.
explanation: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve; technology or input costs shift the whole curve.

trap_notes.default: Own-price changes alter quantity supplied along the curve; input costs and tech shift the supply curve.

items.text: No strategic rivals to react to

prompt: Sort each market-structure trait under pure monopoly or oligopoly.
explanation: A pure monopoly has one seller with no rivals; an oligopoly has a few large firms with strategic interdependence.

trap_notes.default: Monopolies have a single firm; oligopolies have a few dominant rivals that react to one another.

prompt: Sort each welfare measure under consumer surplus or producer surplus.
explanation: Consumer surplus is buyers' net gain below demand and above price; producer surplus is sellers' net gain above supply.

trap_notes.default: Buyers gain when price is below their maximum willingness to pay; sellers gain above marginal cost.

prompt: Sort each government budget trait under balanced budget or budget deficit.
explanation: A balanced budget matches spending to revenue without new borrowing; a deficit spends more than taxes bring in.

trap_notes.default: Deficits occur when annual spending exceeds revenue, requiring Treasury borrowing that adds to debt.

prompt: Sort each stock market trend under bull market or bear market.
explanation: A bull market marks sustained rising prices and optimism; a bear market marks a 20% or deeper decline.

trap_notes.default: Bulls charge upward (rising markets); bears swipe downward (20%+ market drops).

items.text: Private firms plus public safety net

prompt: Sort each economic system trait under traditional or mixed economy.
explanation: Traditional economies follow custom and subsistence; mixed economies combine private markets with government oversight.

trap_notes.default: Custom and barter define traditional economies; private enterprise plus public rules define mixed economies.

items.text: Slice of pizza eaten by one buyer
Extra user costs zero to serve

prompt: Sort each good or trait as rivalrous or non-rivalrous in consumption.
explanation: A rivalrous good is depleted when used by one person; a non-rivalrous good can be shared by many at once.

trap_notes.default: Rivalry asks whether one person's consumption reduces the amount left for others.

prompt: Sort each good or trait as excludable or non-excludable.
explanation: Excludable goods let sellers block non-payers; non-excludable goods benefit everyone regardless of payment.

trap_notes.default: Excludability asks whether providers can feasibly prevent people who do not pay from using the good.
